title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
summary: Giving each process one unbroken block of memory, and the classic first-fit/best-fit/worst-fit placement algorithms that decide which free block a request lands in.

slides.markdown:
The earliest way OSes shared memory across processes was brutally simple: give each process one unbroken chunk, big enough to hold it, and nothing else. No pages, no segments — just a start address and a size.

This model is mostly historical today (paging replaced it decades ago in general-purpose OSes), but it's still the right mental model for understanding **fragmentation**, and it's exactly how allocators like `malloc` manage the heap *inside* a process even now. The placement question it raises — which free block does a new request go into? — reappears everywhere from OS memory management to database storage engines.

slides.sectionTitle: Contiguous allocation: one unbroken chunk per process
slides.markdown:
Under **contiguous memory allocation**, every process's entire address space maps to one continuous range of physical memory — if a process needs 8 MB, the OS finds 8 MB of adjacent free bytes and hands over all of it as a single block.

This makes address translation trivial (it's exactly the base-and-limit scheme from address binding: `physical = base + logical`), which is why it was the standard approach before paging existed. The cost of that simplicity shows up the moment processes start and stop at different times: memory turns into a patchwork of allocated and free chunks of varying sizes, and "find one contiguous range big enough" gets harder over the system's lifetime.

The simplest scheme, **fixed partitioning**, divides memory into a set number of partitions at boot time — say eight partitions of 64 MB each — and each partition holds at most one process.

It's dead simple to implement and the OS's bookkeeping is trivial (just a table of "partition N: free or PID X"). But it wastes memory two ways: a process smaller than its partition wastes the leftover space (internal fragmentation, covered in depth next topic), and a process larger than the biggest partition simply can't run at all, no matter how much total free memory exists elsewhere.

Fixed partitioning is essentially never used in general-purpose OSes today, but it survives in some embedded and real-time systems where predictability matters more than utilization.

**Variable partitioning** drops the fixed boundaries: the OS carves out exactly as much memory as each process asks for, from whatever free space is available, tracked as a list of free "holes" of varying sizes.

When a process exits, its block returns to the free list — and if it's adjacent to another free block, the two get merged into one bigger hole. This fixes fixed partitioning's internal-fragmentation problem (no partition boundary to waste space against) but introduces a new decision the OS has to make on every allocation: **which** hole, among several that are all big enough, should this request go into? That's the placement problem the next few slides answer.

Three classic strategies answer "which hole gets this request?":

- **First-fit** — scan the free list from the start, take the first hole that's big enough. Fast (can stop as soon as it finds one), but tends to fragment the front of memory with small leftover slivers.
- **Best-fit** — scan the *entire* free list, take the smallest hole that's still big enough. Minimizes leftover waste on this one allocation, at the cost of scanning everything every time — and, counterintuitively, it tends to create the smallest, least-reusable leftover slivers overall.
- **Worst-fit** — take the *largest* available hole. The idea is that the leftover remainder stays big enough to be useful for a future request, rather than shrinking into an unusable sliver.

All three are heuristics — none is provably optimal for arbitrary request patterns, which is exactly what the compare slide and simulation below make concrete.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: allocating requests to free blocks under each strategy
slides.markdown:
Free list: `[100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB]` (in address order). Incoming request: **212 KB**.

```text
First-fit:
  scan in order: 100 (too small) -> 500 (fits!) -> stop
  result: takes the 500 KB hole, leaves a 288 KB leftover

Best-fit:
  scan all: candidates >= 212 are 500 and 300
  smallest of those is 300
  result: takes the 300 KB hole, leaves an 88 KB leftover

Worst-fit:
  scan all: largest hole overall is 500
  result: takes the 500 KB hole, leaves a 288 KB leftover
```

Notice first-fit and worst-fit land on the same hole here only because 500 happens to be both "first found" and "largest" — that's a coincidence of this particular free list, not a general rule.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: first-fit vs best-fit vs worst-fit — speed vs fragmentation
slides.markdown:
| | First-fit | Best-fit | Worst-fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scan cost | Stops at first match — fastest | Scans entire free list every time | Scans entire free list every time |
| Leftover sliver size | Medium, unpredictable | Smallest possible — often too small to reuse | Largest possible — often reusable |
| Long-run fragmentation | Moderate; simulations generally show it performs best overall | Tends to litter memory with tiny unusable slivers | Tends to erode all large holes into medium ones, hurting requests that need a big block later |
| Implementation | Simplest | Simple but slower | Simple but slower |

Simulation studies (going back to Knuth) consistently found first-fit and best-fit similar in overall memory utilization, with first-fit faster — worst-fit is generally the weakest of the three despite the appealing intuition behind it.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming best-fit minimizes wasted space overall
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Best-fit finds the tightest fit for each request, so it must waste the least memory overall."

**Why it's wrong:** best-fit optimizes *locally*, per allocation — but tight fits leave tiny leftover slivers (a few KB here, a few there) that are too small for almost any future request. Over many allocations, those slivers accumulate into unusable dead space, even though free-list bookkeeping shows plenty of "free" memory.

**Correct model:** minimizing waste on *this* allocation and minimizing total fragmentation *over the system's lifetime* are different objectives, and they can conflict. This is the general lesson behind why first-fit — which doesn't even try to optimize each allocation — tends to hold up just as well or better in practice.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this still matters: heap allocators and database page allocation
slides.markdown:
General-purpose OSes stopped using contiguous allocation for whole processes once paging arrived — but the exact same first-fit/best-fit tradeoff resurfaces one layer down. A `malloc` implementation manages the heap *inside* one process's address space as a set of variable-size free chunks, and has to answer the identical "which free chunk satisfies this request?" question (more in the heap-allocator topic).

Database storage engines and custom memory pools face the same problem allocating fixed regions of a data file or arena. Whenever you see "first-fit" or "best-fit" mentioned in a systems interview, it's very likely one of these two contexts, not classic whole-process OS allocation — recognizing that context is itself a useful interview signal.
